Mr. Speaker, this is the first time I have the honour of addressing the house. I would like to thank the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the invitation he was so kind as to extend new members on Monday, November 16, to address the house at this very session. Not only does this put us at ease, but it allows me, moreover, to reflect for a moment or so upon certain ideas and principles which will be the basis of my attitude during this session.
I have a very personal reason to congratulate the new Speaker (Mr. Beaudoin). He and I studied together at the faculty of law of the University of Montreal. The honour which he has so richly deserved reflects upon his fellow students in whose name I offer him my best wishes.
As member for the constituency of Maison-neuve-Rosemont I would be remiss in my duty were I not to pay tribute, all too briefly, unfortunately, to my predecessor who now sits in the other place, the Hon. Sarto Fournier. First elected to this house when aged only 26, he now finds himself a senator at the age of 45, having accomplished a very great deal at the beginning of a well filled career which is as yet far from over.
One cannot enjoy the confidence of such an important constituency, for nearly 20 years in succession, without having been a good servant of the people. I believe that the opportunity is well chosen for paying him this tribute, on the occasion of my maiden speech.
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the address allows every hon. member to speak very freely of his constituency; notwithstanding some of my friends' opinions to the contrary, I think it is an excellent idea.
In spite of inevitable repetitions, this debate allows us to familiarize ourselves with the various needs of this country. Canada is not an easy country to govern; its immensity renders its problems often hard to solve and it is all to the credit of the present government to have found a happy formula which makes it a truly national government.
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to represent in this house a constituency of nearly 50,000 electors, of which nearly 20,000 are Englishspeaking. Located in the eastern part of Montreal, which is also known as the metropolis of Canada, that bilingual constituency, made up mostly of workers, of large families, may be held up as a model for the rest of the country. I think that possibly to a higher degree than any other constituency it offers the gratifying reality of a single group, born of two great races, which lives and works in the most complete harmony. Is it not true, Mr. Speaker, that, seen from that angle, Maisonneuve-Rosemont is the very embodiment of the wonderful achievement, possibly the most lasting one, of this government and previous Liberal governments?
National unity is not an empty phrase any more, but is reflected in daily happenings. To illustrate what I have in mind, allow me to mention a fact in particular.
At the beginning of the present session, I became acquainted with members from all parts of the country, and when I mentioned to
418	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Deschatelets some of them who are English-speaking my desire to take advantage of these contacts to improve my knowledge of their tongue, I was pleased to hear them say that they wanted first to improve their own knowledge of the French language.
I was strongly impressed with that fact, and I know that I have already formed with members from both sides a friendship that will endure.
While I was listening to that part of the speech from the throne where it is said that steps will be taken in order that assistance may be granted to totally disabled persons, I thought of the large families I represent here, and I was really proud to be a supporter of this government which has already done so much and intends to do still more for public welfare.
Mr. Speaker, one has to know these districts made up mostly of workers in order to realize what beneficial results the measures enacted by this government have had: yesterday it was old age pensions and family allowances; tomorrow it will be pensions for the disabled. Needless to say subversive ideas do not get very far among our people.
Another measure, possibly the most important of all those mentioned in the speech from the throne, deals with changes to be made in the National Housing Act and the Bank Act, in order to empower our banks and other lending institutions to make mortgage loans.
I cannot help but be acquainted with the housing problem in Montreal, having been for a few years counsel for the rent control board in Quebec. I must say that the housing shortage is possibly more acute in Montreal than in any other city, including Toronto.
There are a great many reasons for this but, in any event, the problem is of the first magnitude. I personally found out, during a survey carried out in Montreal in 1951, that there were almost 100,000 rooms let in that city. In a great many cases they were rented to people who would have had the means to live in proper quarters, had these been available.
Since 1951 the situation has improved enormously and in the northern part of my constituency, in Rosemont, a truly huge housing project is being carried out at the present time. From one week to the next houses are going up. I must give the government its due. Thanks to the housing act it has prevented the development of a catastrophic situation. The loans advanced in that constituency have enormously relieved congestion by creating small housing centres well within the reach of families with modest means.


The forthcoming legislation by improving loan facilities, as forecast in the speech from the throne, will enable a great number of our families to find a home, and I hope that this measure will provide for a low down payment and the longest possible period of amortization.
Coming to another question, may I remind this house that a carriage road, which is the property of the crown, runs through my constituency, along the St. Lawrence, and then crosses the whole city of Montreal.
I know that the traffic problem does not fall under the jurisdiction of the federal authorities but the people of my constituency are the first to suffer from an intolerable situation which is detrimental to progress, and I share the opinion of many experts who say that this carriage road, closed to the public, could help solve partially the traffic problem in Montreal, whether through the construction of an elevated highway or otherwise.
I would not like to venture any suggestion; but if the authorities of the city of Montreal deemed it opportune to approach the federal government in that respect, I would express the wish that their request be sympathetically received.
Mr. Speaker, before I bring my observations in French to a close, I would like to adopt a definite position regarding the matter of fiscal relationship between the federal and the provincial governments-and, more precisely, regarding the autonomy of the province of Quebec. I listened with a great deal of interest to the speeches made in the House of Commons, on Monday, November 16, by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) and on Monday, November 23, by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Dufresne).
I have the highest regard for the views expressed by the hon. gentlemen, but I am afraid I must differ with them. The autonomy of the province of Quebec is an accomplished fact, a fact respected by all, by and large; nobody has ever-neither the present government nor the governments which have preceded it-made any attempt against this autonomy; may I add that it was never less menaced than it is under the present government.
It is not a matter of autonomy and it has never been, but the question has been raised as a pretext; and for this reason, I pity the thousands of electors of my constituency who thus have been inevitably deprived of considerable sums of money to which they are entitled.
If what I say were not the very essence of truth, I would not be here now and the

Progressive Conservative candidate who, in my constituency, advocated the same theory as these two hon. members, would not have lost his deposit on August 10 last.
There are no problems, no matter how complicated they may be, which cannot be solved to the satisfaction of all, when these problems are raised in round-table discussions by men of good will. I am proud to be part of a government composed of men who have demonstrated, up to now, particularly with regard to this question, that they were imbued with the best good will in the world. (Text):
Mr. Speaker, during the last election I promised my English-speaking constituents to improve my English, and this is a promise I am going to fulfil now, even if I am given the privilege of being in the house a further four years.
X would like to make a remark in connection with certain advice directed to new members of this house by the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Fair), in his speech of November 18, as reported at page 146 of Hansard:
On this occasion we have 74 members who are either new to the house or in some cases have been here before but not during the last parliament. I ask them now not to follow the lead of the whip or big boss of the party on all occasions. Let them do their own thinking for once-
Well, I have received a clear mandate to support the government on all good measures brought before this house. I wish to thank my hon. friend for his kind attention, and I hope he will take in good part my own advice, that a member of the opposition should not necessarily be against all good measures proposed by this government. May he act accordingly.
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday the 24th an important group of members of this house visited defence establishments in the Montreal area, and I was glad indeed that one of the highlights of this memorable trip was the inspection of different units and latest models of destroyer escorts and minesweepers at Canadian Vickers Limited. This plant, one of the most important of its kind in this country, is located in my constituency, and I think I express the feelings of my colleagues who attended this inspection in saying that we were more than impressed by what we saw.
Some of these models are original Canadian designs, and we were proud indeed at the thought that in the near future our own Canadian masterpieces will be in service in the defence of our coasts. Our group was led by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), and it is in order that I should thank him for this remarkable initiative. May I also express to Canadian Vickers Limited 83276-27J
The Address-Mr. R. W. Mitchell and to the thousands of anonymous workers at this plant my congratulations for their magnificent achievements.

Mr. Speaker, it is with mixed feelings of fear and humility that I rise to make this, my first speech in this house, and to thereby play my small part in making our form of government, which we call democracy, work. It is a tribute to the genius that is mankind that men and women of all faiths, of many different creeds and of divers political beliefs can come together in comparative harmony and resolve by free and open discussion and debate the problems inherent in a great and growing country.
I need not perhaps stress to hon. members sitting in this house the greatness which is Canada nor the unlimited prospects for a still greater Canada which lie ahead. Nor need I perhaps say that this fusion of peoples of many races, many tongues and many points of view which is called Canada has already assumed a great and responsible place in the council chambers of the world, nor that given proper leadership and guidance we will continue to grow and increase in stature as a world power.
Despite the fact that I probably need not say these things, I am nevertheless going to do so because there are all too few of us in Canada who are prepared to stand on our two feet and express what must be our inward convictions with respect to this great land. We are all too inclined to crawl into a shell when the relative merits or demerits of Canada are discussed. We appear, at least on the surface, to have lost the daring and initiative of our forefathers who carved this land out of the wilderness. It appears to me that we have lost this daring and initiative because we seem to have lost faith in the institutions which our forefathers strove so hard to build up. I suggest that at least part of that lack of faith stems from the reserve which appears to have become innate in us. Here and now I issue a call to all of us who have the honour of sitting in this house and to all who are privileged to call themselves Canadians to rise up and add their voices to those who have been crying in the wilderness of Canadian apathy. Let us shout the name of Canada from the rooftops so that all who will can hear.
Only in this way can we restore to this country the spirit of adventure and daring which we so sadly lack in many sectors and without which we can never go on to the heights of which we are surely capable. Let us get rid of this inferiority complex and gain stature and strength and full belief and
420	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. R. W. Mitchell confidence in ourselves by publicly announcing to the world, and particularly to that great union which lies to the south of our border, that we are a great nation with prospects unequalled in the world. We shall thereby gain assurance and self-confidence to enable us to go on to the summit.
I cannot proceed further without acknowledging the pride and satisfaction which has been previously expressed and which we all feel in the fact that four members of the so-called weaker sex-I think perhaps the word "fairer" is better-have not only answered the call to public service but have been elected to this house. Canada is a nation of home lovers; the family is the centre of activity, and there is ever-increasing evidence of the need for the guidance and counsel of women in public affairs at all levels of government.
I am sure, as I believe all hon. members are sure, that the four ladies who have answered the call will not only serve Canada and Canadians well, but they will by their example also inspire others of charm and ability to further effort. With due respect to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley), I feel I would be remiss if I did not say how particularly delighted I am that three of the four lady members are sitting on this side of the house as members of the opposition.
I acknowledge that I am a neophyte on the floor of this house, and as such I am fully aware of my limitations. I hope I am not presumptuous by nature, Mr. Speaker, but I do wish to associate myself most heartily with those who have spoken before from all parts of the house and who have offered congratulations to you upon your election as Speaker of this house. As a new member I have been most interested in observing your conduct and your actions in presiding over the house, and I can only say that you have exhibited to the full the characteristics of tact and absolute fairness, whilst remaining firm, which your high office demands.
I pursue my course in this house which in some respects at least, and in a much smaller way, will parallel the course which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has set for himself, namely to prod and jab the government. I shall only hope that you will not on too many occasions have to deal with me with that firmness to which I have referred, for it will be my policy to poke and prod at the government on many occasions, although my reasons for doing so will undoubtedly be entirely different from those of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.


Several new members of this house have preceded me in this debate, and I am proud to be one of this particular delegation of freshmen for they have by their conduct in this house set a high standard to follow, and I hope I shall be able in some small way to maintain that standard. My particular congratulations must of course be offered to the hon. members for York Centre (Mr. Holling-worth) and Roberval (Mr. Villeneuve), for it was they who initiated that standard in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
In entering this debate I realize that it is an opportunity for a private member to extol the merits of his or her constituency, and that I believe to be in the best interests of Canada and Canadians. It carries out and puts into effect, at least in part, what I have said earlier, namely that we should continually shout about this country at any and all opportunities; and until we learn to do this about our own particular parts of Canada we will never learn to do it about Canada as a whole.
I have, however, noted with exceeding regret that most hon. members, particularly those from the ranks of the Liberals and C.C.F., have spoiled their effort by coming to this house with their hands out crying of the particular needs of their particular communities and seeking government assistance. They are seeking federal aid for all ailments, some minor and some not so minor, which affect their respective communities. They are all in effect asking the government to step in and subsidize this or subsidize that or take over this or that form of human endeavour. They are all, in other words, encouraging the trend of the present government toward socialism and centralization, and thereby preaching a doctrine which I submit is essentially foreign to the nature of this country and of our ancestors, who built us to what we are purely and simply on courage, initiative and solid belief in free competition.
We have heard speeches by hon. members of this house who represent constituencies ranging from the Atlantic on the east to the Pacific on the west, who represent mighty industries such as fishing, shipbuilding, mining, agriculture and many others which, when combined, endow us with the greatest wealth of natural resources on the face of this earth. Their speeches have been of great interest and assistance in making us realize just how great this country is and just how great are its natural resources. But many hon. members from the parties to which I have just referred have ended up with that note of pathos, asking for help for this or that local problem. As I speak to you briefly at this time of the riding of

London, which I have the honour to represent, I hope I shall not fall into such a pattern, and that I shall not do so in the future except in cases of dire calamity such as flood or tornado.
The city of London is located in the very centre of western Ontario, which has been well described as the garden of Canada. *Western Ontario is not only one of the finest mixed farming areas in Canada but it is also highly industrialized. The outskirts of the city of London are represented in this house by my friend the hon. member for Middlesex East (Mr. White); and the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin), who has the misfortune to sit on the opposite side of this house, has succeeded in wedging his way into a small section of what might, with apologies to my hon. friends from Toronto, be called the metropolitan area of London.
London is a city of widely diversified industry. It produces everything from steel products to paper products. It is the market centre of western Ontario and is in fact the distribution centre for the products, both agricultural and industrial, of the whole of western Ontario. In this connection I wish to raise in the house two points which are of vital interest particularly to London, but also to all of the western Ontario area.
The first of these has to do with the airport at Crumlin, on the outskirts of London, which serves much of the western Ontario area. Most of the freight shipped by air to or from western Ontario passes through the airport at Crumlin, and it has become in this air age essential for the transportation of passengers to and from the larger centres on the continent. Comparatively recently, however, larger and faster aircraft have been introduced into some of the scheduled flights which formerly landed at London. The runways at this airport are not, however, of sufficient length to take care of these newer and larger aircraft, and as a result the air service to western Ontario will have to be curtailed. Already some 'of the flights have been cancelled. I accordingly urge the government to take immediate action to increase the length of these runways and thus restore full air service to the area.
Great sums of money have been spent by the government in building up an air force centre adjacent to this airport. The government has also by its action in increasing the size of Wolseley barracks and establishing a central ordnance depot in the area acknowledged that London is an important and strategic centre; and for this reason I have no hesitation in suggesting to the government
The Address-Mr. R. W. Mitchell that it should fulfil its belief in London by increasing the runways and thereby establishing a proper airport to take care of the traffic which it will be called upon to handle.
The second point also arises with respect to transportation, and has to do with the railway freight rate structure. The board of transport commissioners has been conducting hearings apparently designed to produce a new formula or to do away with or revise the policy which has been in force for many years. This policy briefly provides that shipments to London from the east or from the west and shipments from London to the east 'or to the west can be made at the same rates as those prevailing to or from Toronto. Freight rates, as we are all aware-and particularly hon. members from the west- represent a substantial part of the total cost of manufacturing and distributing our products. London has become, as I have indicated before, a large exporter of manufactured products and an importer of substantial quantities of raw materials for processing in our plants. Many of the industries which have located in London have done so with the assurance that no change would be made in the existing freight rates, so they would be thereby enabled to compete with similar industries in Toronto.
Toronto and some of the larger centres are already congested and overcrowded, and new industry is looking for places to locate outside that city. This is an era of decentralization, and if such decentralization is to continue and thereby reduce the congestion in the larger centres, this government must continue the old established freight rate policy. If that policy is changed new industry will not settle in London, as has been increasingly the case since the war, despite the many advantages which are available to them there. It is not beyond the bounds of possibility that industries presently established may find it impossible to carry on, owing to the high taxation of these days, and may be forced to move to one of the larger centres.
I leave these subjects with the comment that is perhaps obvious; that if the air transportation facilities are not improved or if the freight rate structure is changed, local industry in London will ultimately be affected to an extent that will involve the laying off of many hundreds of Londoners in their plants.
London has six textile mills. I shall not take the time to labour the problems of the textile industry, as they have already been presented to this house in a much more thorough and able manner than I am capable of doing. I shall only say that already two
422	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. R. W. Mitchell of the plants are operating on short hours and three more have ceased production in certain departments, with a consequent serious reduction in wages in the one case and labour in the other.
There is one other problem which affects many cities and towns in Canada but, with the exception of Ottawa, London is more adversely affected by the policy to which I shall refer than almost any other city. The total assessment of federally-owned property in London and its suburbs bears a higher ratio to the total assessment than it does in almost any other city in Canada outside of the national capital. This is perhaps natural because as I have pointed out before, London has not only large army installations but as well has a naval establishment and is the centre in which are located federal government departments for the western Ontario area. The exemption of these properties from municipal taxation accordingly places a higher tax burden on the citizens of London than is placed on those of most other municipalities.
I do not propose to refight the issues of the last election campaign but I do suggest that some change in the present policy must be made, especially in respect of cities such as London, if they are to be able effectively to conduct their local municipal affairs.
It might be interesting to the hon. members of this house to learn that within the last few years the city of London purchased a new pumper for the fire department and of course, in common with other municipalities, paid the usual taxes thereon. The first fire fought by the pumper was at Wolseley barracks, on which the city receives no direct tax revenue from the federal government.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should point out that in addition to being the distribution centre for a highly productive area, and in addition to being a growing and significant industrial city, London is also the seat of the University of Western Ontario. This university has grown and expanded with the times and has made great contributions to cultural, scientific, and business life not only in western Ontario but indeed throughout Canada. We, the citizens of London, shall continue to grow and expand. We shall continue with ingenuity and courage to meet the problems with which we are confronted; and, with apologies to my hon. friends from the Toronto area, we shall continue to display the same quality of intestinal fortitude as was displayed by the Western football team on Saturday last in Toronto, with the result that our future as a great Canadian city is secure.

Mr. Deputy Speaker, in rising to speak on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and rising for the first time in this House of Commons, I am privileged to offer you my congratulations on your appointment. Your qualifications and ability are well known to the veteran members of the house. May I ask you to transmit my congratulations to Mr. Speaker on his election to his honoured post.	Our
Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was well advised when on the opening day of the first session of the twenty-second parliament he moved that Mr. Speaker take the chair of the house as our Speaker. Since this debate began he has proven to us that he possesses in high degree the qualifications required to fill this role.
We new members of the House of Commons were also honoured and pleased when we listened to the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I extend congratulations to the hon. member for York Centre and to his colleague, the hon. member for Roberval, for their magnificent presentations to the house in moving and seconding the adoption of the speech from the throne.
We have had reasons for rejoicing since the prorogation of the twenty-first parliament in May last. The coronation of our beloved Queen of Canada, Elizabeth II, was an occasion for universal rejoicing. Her Majesty holds a warm place in the hearts of all her subjects, and her devotion to duty together with her personal charm have strengthened our attachment to the crown. May I join with millions of her subjects in wishing her much joy and happiness in the long journey she and her husband are now undertaking throughout the commonwealth.
We, at least those of us sitting on the government side of the house, had different reasons for rejoicing on the evening of August 10 last when the Canadian electorate expressed in such an overwhelming manner its desire to have our great leader the Prime Minister and his government administer the affairs of this country for the next four years. As a newly elected member of the House of Commons I am amazed at all the superfluous excuses brought forward by some hon. members of Her Majesty's opposition in trying to account or answer for the defeat of their respective parties. While some hon. members have even intimated that there was no difference between the four major parties forming this present parliament, we Liberals will realize that we are here because we have a great leader and a great cabinet, and

we represent a party which embraces well defined principles applicable to every aspect of life whether social, political or economic.
In his address to the house on Friday, November 20, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) deplored the condition of public piers along Saint John harbour. He described the dock as an eyesore of rotting and moulding timber. Before making such declarations I wonder if my hon. friend took the time to glance at the public works accounts for the last four years. If he had taken the time to do so he would have found that over $7 million was spent on public works in his own constituency from 1949 to 1952. Furthermore, when on November 20 the newspaper L'Evangeline of Moncton was reporting on page 1 an account of the hon. member's remarks in this house, on page 2 of the same issue was a statement from the chairman of the national harbours board announcing that over $2,500,000 would be spent for further improvement of the port of Saint John during 1954. I would feel proud and happy if during the next four years my constituency of Gloucester could be neglected as much as the hon. member claims that Saint John-Albert has been. We in Gloucester county would welcome public works expenditures to the extent of over $1,500,000 per year for the next four or five years.
I agree with the statement made to this house by the hon. member for Victoria-Carle-ton (Mr. Montgomery) with regard to the urgent need for cheap hydroelectric power in New Brunswick. We all realize that cheap power is the key to industry and a well balanced economy. The hon. member asked why New Brunswick has not developed more of her available resources. It is true that shortage of power has been the main factor causing lack of industries in our province, but we are forced to realize that in 1925 the government in power in the province of New Brunswick sold or practically gave away to private enterprise, particularly to United States interests, the most important source of energy on the Saint John river, namely the power site at Grand Falls. New Brunswick is paying dearly today for this most unwise and undesirable move.
My friend the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) has once more brought to the attention of the house an important subject which is of great interest to all of us in New Brunswick. I am referring to the proposed Passamaquoddy bay power project. Since 1935 not only this house, not only the New Brunswick legislature, but even the government of the United States have on numerous occasions discussed or taken partial action toward ascertaining the feasibility of this
The Address-Mr. Robichaud grandiose project. I adhere strongly to the hon. member's suggestion that action should be taken to find out once and for all if the realization of this project is reasonably and economically sound.
While on the question of power may I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to bring to the attention of this house another project of major importance which also on many occasions has been a theme of discussion, namely the Chignecto canal. We in New Brunswick were pleased to hear in the speech from the throne that the New York state power authority had accepted a licence for the development of the United States share of power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river. We have the interest and welfare of the whole nation at heart and we will support this project of a national character. In view of the important mining developments taking place in my constituency of Gloucester, I feel that the time is most opportune to emphasize the need for the earliest possible action toward the realization of this long talked about project, the Chignecto canal.
It was proven long ago that such a canal would be a valuable asset in time of war and also of great value in a period of peace. The cost of transportation from northern New Brunswick of minerals, pulp, lumber, fish, potatoes and other agricultural products would be greatly reduced, to the benefit of the producers of these products, if the project could be completed. In addition, its construction would provide a considerable amount of employment at a period when the situation in the maritimes is not too rosy. I fully support and concur in the suggestions of the hon. members for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) and Cumberland (Mr. Lusby), who dealt with this question.
In my maiden speech before this house I should like to say a few words about my constituency. Gloucester, with its 200 miles of shore line, is beautifully located in the northeastern corner of New Brunswick, extending along the blue and salty waters of the baie de Chaleur and the gulf of St. Lawrence. These waters are richly populated with fish of all varieties such as lobsters, clams, salmon, cod, haddock, flounders, herring, mackerel, smelts, and we must not overlook the famous Caraquet and Shippigan oysters. These are among my county's most popular varieties of fish and shellfish.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel humble and honoured to have this opportunity of speaking for the first time in the House of Commons. From the very outset I have listened with a great deal of interest to the flow of debate from both sides of this house, and especially to the ideas which have been brought forward as the key and solution to the great problems which face our nation.
During the first days of this session of the twenty-second parliament, it was my great pleasure to witness two memorable events, both of which contained messages for each and all of us. They were not messages of partisanship, for that is not important; nor were they messages of momentary importance.


They reflected rather the basic purpose of parliament as well as basic faiths which we as a people believe in. As a new member I make reference to them, Mr. Speaker, with modesty, for I am fully aware that hon. members are deeply conscious of their significance. I do so first because they impressed me, and also because it sometimes happens that because of our closeness to a situation we take certain features for granted, and in doing that we fail to be guided by them in our decisions.
The first was the thrill of participating as a new member in the opening ceremonies of this house, in the age-old tradition of selecting our Speaker and hearing his humble and meaningful words of acceptance. These and the subsequent -colourful event in the Senate chamber vividly drew to our minds -the simple principles upon which are built the constitutional way of our life and the free institutions- which our people -cherish above -all things.
The ceremony, the words spoken, Mr. Speaker, symbolized forcefully that political power is not permanent, nor is it absolute, nor is it centralized, but rather diffused and-variable and at all times qualified and subject to the decisions of the representatives of the people-and in the light of what is happening in the world today, wherein few people remain who have retained the rights of unfettered discussion, thereby being able to check abuse and bring betterment-only then can we fully appreciate o-ur political way of life.
There are few places remaining where men -are politically free, and our assembly should remember this. It -calls for each of us, and in particular the government, to make our activities in this parliament a shining example of what free men can accomplish. Freedom has a very bad habit of slipping away when we take it for granted -and leave it unguarded.
The second memorable event was the visit and address in this chamber by the President of the United States, Mr. Eisenhower. His inspiring address touched on many of the physical problems facing our two nations. I am sure we can resolve them provided that we use common sense and are sincere, and provided also that both sides realize fully that the well-being of one is the well-being of the other, and that the weakness of one might well be a source of danger to the strength of the other.
I was particularly interested in the theme of the President's address, the theme which ran repeatedly through his message, which reminded us of the lesson implied in the

opening ceremonies of this house. It was his reference to moral and spiritual principles. I should like to quote two passages:
Our primary reliance is a unity among us forged of common adherence to moral principles. This reliance binds together in fellowship all those who believe in the spiritual nature of man, as the child of God.
Then a little further on he had this to say:
We have to hand over to those who come after us this balance of values, and particularly the certainty that they can enjoy the same kind of opportunity in this spiritual, intellectual and material world that we, who will then be their ancestors, enjoyed before them. That, it seems to me, is the real problem that Canada and the United States today face together. It is one reason I get such a thrill every time I come to this country, because here I sense in the very atmosphere your determination to work in that direction, not acknowledging defeat, certain that we can win, because there are values that man treasures above all things else in the world.
Mr. Speaker, the enormous truth in the words of the United States President calls for an equivalent response by all who hold office and responsibility. I am one of those who believe that many of our problems, the chaos in which the world finds itself, is the accumulative result of man's indifference to the practical application in his affairs of these principles. It is not enough to profess allegiance to those principles. What is far more important is that we be guided by them. We live in an age of uncertainty and fear. Why? Because in the great struggle of ideologies presently being waged between communism and private enterprise we do not seem to understand that there is a third force waiting to be recognized and capable of solving many of man's dilemmas. This is the force of spiritual principles, and more specifically speaking the good and the positive in action.
When we read in the daily press of the scandalous betrayals by men in high office, men who were entrusted with the confidence of their people, when we observe the strife and the bloodshed in this tired world of ours, surely it becomes clear that fundamentally these are the results of the refusal to recognize that the building of a just and worthwhile social order can only be on the foundation of moral and spiritual integrity.
There is no other road to economic strength; there is no other way to have agreement. It is the only way to have peace; and all of this, Mr. Speaker, resolves itself into the fact that we of this generation are living at a time in human history when man is truly being challenged. We are being challenged to repair quickly the imperfections of our social order, or we shall continue to watch the ever-increasing collapse of human structures.
I say that the choice of policies which faces this house is no different from the 83276-284
The Address-Mr. Holowach choice of policies which faces us as individuals. What is that choice? It is simply this:	either policies which will
promote independence, policies devoted to the well-being of the individual and the sovereignty of people and nations, or policies which regiment the individual and enslave nations; either the best interests of all the people of Canada regardless of where they live or who they are, or policies of patronage and the well-being of political machines and pressure groups; either real prosperity based on the people's ability to acquire the God-given abundance of our land and production, or policies which deny them these things and create want and unemployment; either simplicity, sincerity and honesty, or red tape, arrogance and incompetence; either putting into practice the precept of as little government as possible, 'or the extravaganza of more and more centralized government; either giving a real deal to our producers, workers, farmers, veterans, aged and disabled, or a patchwork of remedies which perhaps appease for the moment but which belie our lip service to humanity; either policies which will once again make fashionable the old virtue of frugality in government, or policies which are not without waste and extravagance.
These are the choices. One is positive, the other is negative; one uses the practical approach, the other is a visionary, theoretical concept; one is based on hard truth, the other is the much easier road of expediency.
I should like now to make a few general remarks related to the subjects mentioned in the throne address. As I travelled from the great northwest to attend this session of our twenty-second parliament one single thought dominated my feeling. I was thinking of the untold opportunities which exist for us to make Canada a model nation for others to follow. It was the feeling of vastness and of the immeasurable abundance of our land.
With those thoughts in mind the question arises, is there any rhyme or reason why, at least in this part of the world, there should be want when we have so much of everything, or unemployment when there is so much to be done? What justification is there to deny people who are physically handicapped more than the meagre pittance presently handed out to them? If in time of war billions are available for destruction, why is it that in times of peace millions of our people and many businesses have to suffer economic instability and recession?
Is there any reason why an abundance of food, meat, fish, fruit and materials should
428	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Holowach be, as it is now, a source of anxiety and concern as to their disposition, rather than being the blessing which they really are? What is wrong with sharing these great surpluses with our own Canadian people? This could be done by maintaining effective purchasing power in circulation so the goods needed could be acquired by our people. What seems so wrong with exchanging the balance of surpluses over and above our requirements with less fortunate countries which could in turn make payment in goods they have in excess? I agree with those who have said that such a gesture would remove many of the causes of war brought about by struggles for markets and the erection of financial barriers, or efforts to acquire food and raw materials which the people need.
I propose that the following principles be adopted in connection with our foreign trade policy; first, the home market to be provided with purchasing power sufficient for Canadians to buy our domestic goods and products at reasonable prices; second, make available to nations whose domestic needs require them, under reasonable and fair conditions, the food and raw materials of which Canada may have an abundance; third, encourage trade by a policy under which our surplus goods will be exchanged on a basis of mutual advantage and in an effort to avoid cutthroat competition; fourth, remove all those trade barriers which have arisen out of the operation of the present system and which permit international transactions which are not in the interests of all the people of Canada.
I was pleased to read in the throne speech that the government intended to further tackle the serious situation created by the housing shortage. All of us will welcome speedy measures to alleviate this situation. I think we will also agree that there is no excuse for its existence. The only time it would appear justified is when there were no materials or skills with which to build homes. We can understand the heavily-populated areas of Great Britain or nations such as Germany, France, Italy, Israel and Greece having housing problems, but that certainly should not be so in Canada.
One would have to stretch one's imagination to the breaking point to find a good excuse for the existence of the acute housing situation in this country, in view of the few millions of people living here. Every Canadian should be given the means of securing a comfortable and beautiful home. Happy homes for our people will defend us much more than will the instruments of war. People


are our greatest assets, and more homes will bring the happy and natural consequence of more population.
Let us remember that one of the reasons for this deplorable shortage of houses is that during the years of depression money alone was scarce. Although labour and building materials were plentiful, the shortage of money prevented normal house building for over ten years. May I therefore submit that if we are to reduce the growing number who say or imply that democracy cannot bring fulfilment, that the future belongs to another concept of man and his fate, then young men and women of limited capital should not be denied homes and shelter. I therefore propose that in this parliament legislation be introduced which will induce and encourage every citizen to build and own a home by providing the very lowest of monthly payments, the very minimum of down payments, and at cost.
As I have mentioned before, I have listened with interest to the ideas incorporated in these discussions. We need not have "isms" if we apply ourselves intelligently to the task of repairing our social imperfections. What we need is more democracy with a freer economy, with policies that induce creative qualities in people, something far removed from the compulsions and arbitrary directives with which our people presently are being bombarded.
What is needed is not new methods or new ways. We need new vision. Yes, this section of the house believes in and champions the cause of private competitive enterprise. We will always be against the superman theory of state regimentation. Why? Because the greatest social and economic progress the world has ever seen has been achieved in this way. Our strength and our national well-being depend on our production. Industry produces more when it is free than it does when it is regimented. It provides more jobs, higher wages, cheaper goods and better goods when it is induced by individual initiative.
Today the problems facing us are not the result of individual enterprise having failed. Its job is to produce. It is our government which has failed in making possible the distribution of the abundance produced by private enterprise. Because of this I propose immediate and progressive reduction of taxation on individual earnings, on cooperatives and on business. This will induce reinvestment and stimulate economic and industrial development which in turn will

progressively raise living standards and give opportunities for gainful employment.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell you something of the area which I have the honour to represent. Though at times hon. members on the opposite side of this house may differ with the views expressed by our section, I am sure the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) will agree with my remarks.
The city of Edmonton is not only one of the fastest growing and most vigorous communities of Canada, it is also the capital city of the great province of Alberta. Judging from the talk of the people outside our province, no other part of Canada symbolizes more forcefully the idea of progress and progressive government than do the city of Edmonton and the province of Alberta. East and west the talk is of the financial stability of our province, its people, the ever-growing industrial development of that area and its potential. I think it is no exaggeration to say that nowhere on the North American continent has more attention been focused.
Here is a land blessed with raw materials far in excess of our present requirements. Here is an area which has just begun to flex its industrial muscles. The nation's leading magazines write of the phenomenal Alberta story. It is no wonder; it is phenomenal. In this province Canada and the world are beginning to see something more than outstanding achievement. They are beginning to see the ideas and principles backing those achievements. Here is the birthplace of a people's Social Credit government. In brief, it is the place where the government of a people have written a record of service which commands the respect and recognition of all fairminded people who are impressed with honesty, order and social progress. This story of Alberta's success is a result of the people of that province backing a government whose policies are dedicated to giving the people the results they want through the proper and efficient management of their affairs. Believe you me, sir, we Albertans know where we are going.
I wish this house to know something about my constituency. Since it is an integral part of our city of Edmonton, I shall speak of Edmonton itself. There are over 150 years of history behind Edmonton. What was once a small trading post is today an ever-growing metropolis spread over an area of about 42 J square miles. It is the gateway to the vast riches of the Peace river country and our northern empire. It is the crossroads of world aviation. It is an industrial giant.
The Address-Mr. Holowach Located in the heart of Canada's largest oil and natural gas fields, Edmonton is the focal point of an industry which has converted 90 per cent dependency with respect to our nation's oil requirements to a position of near self-sufficiency. The $55 million cela-nese plant, the $13,500,000 Canadian Industries Limited plant and numerous refineries are located there. The Interprovincial pipe line and the Trans Mountain pipe line have their beginning in Edmonton. Edmonton has confidence in Canada and our ability to do things. Both labour and management share this view and provide teamwork.
Despite this industry, however, agriculture is the basis of the province's and the city's economy. For this reason the welfare of our farmer citizens is of grave concern to our city people, for the farmers' welfare transposes itself on the general well-being of the constituents of Edmonton East. Edmonton East is the home of large meat processing plants, and through this area are channelled many of the primary products from our lakes, rivers, forest and mines.
I should like to tell you something of our greatest asset, namely the people who live in my constituency. They are people of many races and creeds. They include men and women from the British Isles, men and women of Ukrainian, French, German, Italian, Jewish, Greek, Polish, Slavic and Chinese origin, each rightfully proud of his or her racial heritage but each fervently proud to be a Canadian first. They are an alert and creative people. They work hard and play hard. My constituency is one of Canada's great athletic centres with an unrivalled general sports enthusiasm. You have all heard of the Edmonton Eskimos. My people are industrious and love, too, the arts and the gracious things of life.
By occupation the majority of my constituents are industrial and business workers. As such they have facing them as citizens many specific problems I shall bring to the attention of this house on future occasions. My constituency of Edmonton East has many problems arising from the rapid growth of our city. These problems require sympathetic consideration by the federal authorities. Here is only one example. The town of Beverly, bordering the eastern outskirts of Edmonton, is in fact a most important part of my constituency. It is a vigorous and ever-expanding residential and business area. The people of Beverly rightfully feel that the present postal facilities and services, while perhaps satisfactory in years gone by, are now inadequate and do not meet the needs of the people. In view of the tremendous

The Address-Mr. Holowach expansion of this area the people of Beverly desire the inauguration of postal delivery service.
In a general way, Mr. Speaker, my constituents are deeply concerned over the long and heavy burden of taxes which have been imposed upon them and the people of Canada by this government. They are concerned with their financial inability to acquire homes which they need on a satisfactory and equitable basis. They are concerned with the high cost of living and inflation which is daily erasing their hard-earned savings and rewards of labour. Inflation must be halted and taxes reduced, for those who suffer are the workers on fixed salaries and budgets, the housewives, pensioners, veterans, and countless others. The government is responsible for this situation by its policies of hidden taxes on just about everything we buy. The burden has fallen on the poor, those least able to protest against this inequitable situation.
My constituents are concerned with the ever-mounting debt of our nation which places liabilities upon generations yet unborn. They feel there should be no political patronage in the matter of selection to high offices in our land. They are concerned with the government's delays in rectifying discriminating policies, as in the matter of freight rates which go into the cost of the things they buy and what they ship to market, and retard the growth of our industrial development. My constituents are concerned with what they consider unsatisfactory and beggarly treatment of our aged, our blind, our veterans and our disabled in the matter of their pensions. In this connection may I quote a short passage from a letter received from the executive officer of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind in the city of Edmonton:
Under the Blind Persons Act, sightless Canadians may receive a blindness allowance subject to a very rigid means test which limits a single person to an annual income of $840 including the allowance and a married recipient to $1,320. Obviously, these totals are drastically inadequate and leave no room for self-improvement.
My people, Mr. Speaker, are interested in humanity, not politics, and I should like to go on record as supporting their demands. My constituents watch with care the activities of our central government and desire to see the arrest of waste and extravagance. In this respect I have in my hand a communication directed to me by the Edmonton chamber of commerce which reads in part as follows:
That the Edmonton chamber of commerce deplores the action of the federal government in extending the activities of the national film board in competition with private enterprise:	and
further, that it is opposed to this large expenditure
{Mr. Holowach.]
of public moneys, creating more jobs for civil servants which could be absorbed in private industry; and, further, that this opinion be conveyed to the Ottawa board of trade, the three Edmonton members of parliament and the Canadian chamber of commerce.
Before resuming my seat I should like, Mr. Speaker, to perform one duty. I would be reluctant to speak on this matter were it not that statements made were void of truth and fair play. What I have to say is in direct reply to the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode). I am sure he is an honourable man and welcomes correction. Speaking on Friday, November 20, he gave an interpretation to a statement supposedly made by the premier of Alberta.
Canada has had many distinguished sons and daughters, but none has ever commanded more love and admiration from the people than does the premier of Alberta. Few statesmen have distinguished themselves more in the cause of social justice. Millions see in him a man of the highest Christian integrity and honesty, and their champion in the cause of humanity. The youngest premier in the British commonwealth of nations, he is beloved by the people of Alberta whose leader and spokesman he is. Even now history records his outstanding contribution to the social, economic and political progress of our nation.
To my way of thinking, the newspaper clipping read into Hansard is unfair and untrue. It quotes a few short sentences of a 45-minute address which lauded the virtues of the British people as a shining example for men .and nations to follow. I know, for I was there. I heard him speak. In fact the essence of this clipping creates an impression diametrically opposed to the positive message in the premier's address.
It was disappointing that the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna), who spoke yesterday evening, allowed himself, in the latter part of his speech, to be misguided into casting reflection upon the extraordinary economic and financial accomplishments of his own province. I was surprised that the hon. member did not get the facts before he spoke, because if he had his speech would have been a good one. I could have given him the facts if he had asked me.

The hon. member himself
said the city of Edmonton had been the fastest-growing city in all Canada for the past several years. Everyone knows that when a city doubles its population in less than ten years it puts a terrific strain on the services and facilities the city is forced to supply to its residents. Consequently there would have to be a tremendous upsurge in

borrowing in order to provide those facilities. It is true that Edmonton's debt has increased. But what the hon. member did not tell the house is that between $3 million and $3J million of Edmonton's debt was borrowed from the provincial government at 2 per cent under a self-liquidating projects scheme for a period of 20 years.
Last year the city borrowed from the provincial government $9 million at rates that ran from 2 to 3J per -cent depending on the nature of the projects involved and the term. Some of this money was borrowed for 25 years. Moreover, last year the provincial government bought up $11 million of debentures of the two cities of Calgary and Edmonton at 31 per cent, which saved all the handling costs that usually are incurred when debentures are handled through financial houses. Next year my city expects to borrow another $12 million from the provincial government at rates running from 2J to 3| per cent for various projects of expanding utilities and services.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, our young country with its wealth and wonders of production, with the creative qualities of its everyday people, coupled with sound, sensible policies, can make this age in which you and1 I live not only one of peace but of happy living. This section of the house stands for homes, not promises. It stands for jobs, not relief. It stands for what is right, not who is right. It stands for peace without poverty. We are united in our purpose, we are strengthened by the conviction that our principles of life and government are the only practical alternative for the people of Canada, and we are advancing.
