speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoy very much being called upon to speak on a Friday evening because I have a feeling that we may address ourselves in a loud voice.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, you will not be surprised if I do not spare you my compliments nor my congratulations, for compliments are like flowers; if we add new flowers to those that are already cut, the bouquet becomes but more beautiful and its perfume more pleasant. You will also allow me to tell you that your personality, your spirit of justice and especially your experience in the discussion of diplomatic affairs, were calling you to the high function that you now occupy. I am sure that
The Address-Mr. Boisvert the confidence unanimously placed in you by the various parties will be justified, thanks to a competence which will always remind us of your predecessor's, which you will strive to imitate, in order to do even better.
I should not like to remain silent about the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Robinson) who now occupies the position of Deputy Speaker and whom I have known especially as chairman of the committee on radio broadcasting. He gave us proof that he is a remarkable public man and, above all, he has demonstrated that he could give the impression that everybody was right, without saying that anyone was wrong.
I also wish to congratulate the two hon. members who have moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did so in well-chosen words and in such a way that those who have elected them must feel honoured in having done so.
It would be appropriate also to congratulate the newly appointed ministers and parliamentary assistants. They will constitute a new pleiad which can only be of benefit to the nation's business, in view of their experience and devotion to the commonwealth.
Finally, I must mention the subject of the re-election of the government, and pay tribute to the Prime Minister. His knowledge of affairs and human beings makes him one of the first citizens of the world. His qualities of heart and experience allow him to tower above the Canadian scene with rare merit. His colleagues of the cabinet do not see in him merely a leader to be obeyed, but a friend who endeavours to maintain the prestige of everyone, in order to uphold the prestige of our country. Personally, it is to the Prime Minister that I owe my re-election and I am proud of it. I am also grateful to all those who have helped me with their words and eloquence.
I should like now to touch upon some of the problems concerning the political and economic life of the country. First of all, I must say I am glad to note in the speech from the throne that an effort will be made, and I quote:
As further steps in helping to improve social welfare, co-ordinated plans for rehabilitation of disabled persons are being worked out with the provinces and a measure to facilitate the establishment nation-wide of a federal-provincial assistance program for totally disabled persons will be submitted for your consideration.

The Address-Mr. Boisvert
On many occasions, since 1949, I have spoken before this house and elsewhere in favour of those unfortunate people who are not responsible for their affliction and who suffer to the bottom of their hearts from pangs of despair often worse than their disability. The Liberal party, which has always been in the vanguard of social legislation in this country, will take pride in bringing to these unfortunate people some degree of comfort, if not perfect, at least sufficient to remove from their minds any impression of being outcasts.
I am happy too that the St. Lawrence seaway project along with its hydroelectric development will be carried out in the years to come. This hydroelectric development, as well as the opening of a channel which will enable deep-sea ships to reach as far as the lakehead will bring to Canada as yet incalculable political and economic benefits. It is with satisfaction that I have found the following passage in the report of the Canadian maritime commission:
Growing interest in the St. Lawrence seaway project is reflected in the expansion of direct shipping services between the great lakes and overseas. In 1952, vessels registered outside Canada and the United States made 338 passages with cargo through the St. Lawrence canals. This figure compares with 222 in 1951 and 202 in 1950.
This quotation is sufficient to demonstrate the interest this matter has created, not only in Canada and the United States, but the world over. It will be recalled that all the great discoverers who came to the new world were looking for a passage to India or China. The Panama canal was opened so as to enable communication to be established, by way of the Americas, from Europe to Asia. When shipping reaches the lakehead the dream that Cartier had in 1534 of reaching the Pacific by following the St. Lawrence river will have been half realized.
The idea of crossing continents by interior waterways is as old as the world. Rivers have been called "roads that move". The first real progress to be made in this world can be ascribed to the existence of this method of transportation.
In every country the great capitals are almost always located along a river. Paris is on the Seine, London on the Thames. I could go on indefinitely describing all the world's great capitals situated on rivers or at their mouths.
It is with gratification that we have learned that the Canadian government have taken upon themselves to proceed with the St. Lawrence seaway plan so that this river may become the most important inland waterway in the world. The beauty of the river and its
[Mr. Boisvert.l
economic and industrial possibilities will help to sustain the industrial growth which is characteristic of Canada today, as well as of the whole world.
Allow me now to take up a subject of local interest.
As long as this project has not been realized I do not think it would be possible to proceed with the immediate construction of a bridge which would join my constituency to that represented by the hon. member for Three Rivers, even though I favour this project.
Present circumstances are not such that they allow for the immediate implementation of this project and the hon. member for Three Rivers knows it. I am in favour of those public works which bring about a quick and practical solution to the problems relating to the social welfare and advancement of the people living in a certain area. But such works, whichever government undertakes them, must be undertaken in accordance with our constitution. When it comes to public works, it is necessary to know first if the plans are workable, what the cost will be and then who, according to our political system, will bear the cost. We must wonder whether it should be the municipalities, or the provincial government, or the federal government. I might add, in jest of course, that should the construction of a bridge be left to the provincial authorities, it might not remain standing for a great number of years. We have known that kind of thing to happen.
The government of Canada has built at Ste. Angele de Laval, in my county, a most modern wharf. It will be up to the city of Three Rivers to provide a ferry service that will answer the needs of the people in my county and the surrounding counties.
I recall that the hon. member for Three Rivers-and I am sorry he is not here this evening-criticized me and the government with regard to the carrying out of extensive works in Nicolet, for a gun proving range. He has even campaigned in my constituency, claiming we were going to ruin agriculture. Three Rivers was bom and has grown and yet I have never heard it said that the farmers of the district had had cause for complaint.
Since the federal government has spent several million dollars, of which two-thirds were left in my constituency, property has increased in value. The population is now growing instead of decreasing at an alarming rate, and the revenues of the customs department and the Post Office Department are larger.

The hon. member for Three Rivers in his eagerness to play politics at my expense -I do not blame him for it-forgot that what is good for the district of Nicolet is also good for the city of Three Rivers.
At a time when there was unemployment in Three Rivers, I saw somewhere that retail sales in the city of Three Rivers were going up for the year. Had it not been for the public works carried out in my constituency, this would not have been possible and I would like the hon. member from now on to remember that what is good for Nicolet is also good for Three Rivers, and that when the member for Nicolet works for the county of Nicolet-Yamaska he works at the same time for the county represented by the hon. member for Three Rivers. I may add that when the time comes to link the south shore to the north shore of the St. Lawrence, the government of Canada will be only too glad to help with the carrying out of any project acceptable to the proper authorities, and the member for Nicolet-Yamaska will not fail, and without playing politics, to suggest and to support such a project, as long as it is to the advantage of the people of the county of Nicolet-Yamaska and of the central part of the province of Quebec. (Text):
Before making a few remarks about the United Nations where I spent eight weeks, for which I warmly thank the government, I should like to speak about a matter that is bothering the democratic conscience of the free world. That matter deals with production.
Farmers are complaining about the fall in the prices of their products. This phenomenon is more pronounced in the United States than in Canada. On the other hand, in cities and towns people are complaining about the increases in prices of both agricultural and manufactured goods. The groups that oppose each other and oppose the Liberal party in this House of Commons are seeking, through insidious propaganda, to hold the Canadian government responsible for that condition.
Some say in short that the government meddles too much with matters that are not within its jurisdiction; others say the government is not taking as active an interest as it should take in matters that are within its province; finally another group contends, which is simple, and oversimple, that we should revamp our banking and monetary system which, as we know, is tied closely to the exchange problem and has a constant and direct relationship with trade between the various countries of the world.
This is an important problem that should receive our serious consideration. In my
The Address-Mr. Boisvert humble opinion it is at the very foundation of our economic activity, and is characterized at the present time by the struggle between capital and labour which determines the contingencies of an ill-balanced and day to day economy.
Figures tell us that weekly hours of work tend to decrease. There are only 4l-l hours in the present work week. On the other hand the trend of weekly wages is exactly the opposite. They tend to increase from month to month. During the past year they have increased in the manufacturing industry by an average of nearly $2 a week. I believe this indicates a defect in the operation of the economic machinery, because those who supply the food to our people are not treated in the same way as those whom they feed with the produce of their farms. Work on the farm is work, just the same as the work of those who are employed in manufacturing, mining, transportation, the building industries, and so on.
As a result the cost of producing foodstuffs is getting higher and higher, in a way that is detrimental to the farmers and other working classes, while the cost of consumer goods weighs heavily on the workingman's budget. I think one of the best remedies for the problem would be to increase the real volume of production. This can be brought about only by working longer hours in the factories, and by greater diligence and a deeper interest in the community at large.
If we could place a larger quantity of goods at the disposal of our people, the demand would not be as great and prices would tend to fall. I am far from suggesting that the worker has no right to his share-and a large one-in progress, both for his own benefit and that of his family. On the contrary I would like to see him enjoy earthly possessions, and see him happy. However, he must not lose sight of the new responsibilities toward society as a whole which result from the right to associate, and the importance of measuring nowadays with greater foresightedness the consequences of his conduct; because those consequences will be judged by an experienced, fault-finding and responsive public opinion.
One must be very wise when half the people on earth are fear-stricken and the other half poverty-stricken. It would be disastrous to wait until our country is in the throes of a depression, or our cities are struck off the map of the world, to realize that work is the first lot imposed on man by God, and that work well done is an achievement of the civilization to which we are proud to belong.

The Address-Mr. Boisvert
An American industrialist wrote recently:
We may seek for ourselves a maximum of opportunities, but we must stop when we are about to cause prejudice to others. It is up to us to find out when we have to stop. Abuses are what make laws necessary. It is only when citizens go beyond the limits set by their conscience that the government must step in. Consequently, the less we stay within certain limits, the more we will be forced to rely on the government and the more likely we will be to fall prey to socialism.
We must preserve this dynamic force which we possess. In some forms of society, man is bound to his work by the fear of the whip. In this country, everyone is bound to his work by the consciousness of relations between one's own interest and the interest of the community. But if the interest of the individual happens to be detrimental to the interest of the community, the legislator must then step in. Consequently, the more we will abuse our liberty, the more numerous will be our laws and the more unavoidable will be socialization.
The philosophy of a minimum of effort and a maximum of financial return, which leads the masses to believe erroneously that the welfare of man is based on the wages earned and received at the end of each week, goes along with another philosophy which is the philosophy of industrial production. The motto of our times seems to be an ever-increasing production. This principle has been expressed in the speech from the throne before the Quebec legislative assembly. May I quote three typical excerpts:
A remarkable fact is that the province enjoys an extraordinary prosperity . . .
For the past few years, it has known a tremendous development, which is ever-increasing, and which promises an extraordinary, solid and lasting progress . . .
The progressive and well-defined policy set by my government recognizes the necessity of industrial progress.
Those quotations make it obvious that the Quebec legislature is going all-out for industrial progress, and I blame no one at all. However, industrial progress is not everything; far from it. Here is an incident which occurred during my stay in New York. One of the first delegates I happened to meet was a congressman. He struck me as being a charming man, with a strong personality and endowed with many qualities. When I was introduced to him he soon saw I was of French descent and French-speaking. He said, "Oh, you are from that part of Canada which would like to be independent." I said, "What do you mean?" He replied, "Is it not a fact that the province of Quebec wishes to leave the Canadian confederation?" "Where did you get such ideas?" I asked him with surprise. He told me that something he had read had given him that impression.

I answered, "But there is nothing farther from the truth, considering the political history of Canada since confederation". "Confederation", I added, "was achieved by Canadians, both of British and French origin. Since 1896 the province of Quebec has been faithful to the Liberal party; and it is because it has supported, always with very large majorities, the Liberal party that the same party has for 43 years been leading the country. Since the unity of Canada is a fact, in the framework of confederation; since 1867 Canada has made giant strides toward absolute independence and Canadian sovereignty; since Canada, once a colony, has become a powerful nation, benefiting from a politically sound administration and a well-balanced economy, is it not an error to claim that Quebec is not well off in the confederation?" I added, "Since the end of the last century the province of Quebec has given Canada two prime ministers of French descent: the first one, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, laid the foundation of the nation; the second, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, increased the Canadian territory when he admitted Newfoundland into the confederation; and, under him, Canada, instead of being the vassal of another country, has become a nation which plays in the world a part far more important than we would expect from such a small population".
It was the turn of my interlocutor to be amazed. We then parted company.
I would not have mentioned this incident, if it had been an isolated case. But I regret to say that, though I never witnessed any unfairness, I found in other American circles a remarkable ignorance of the existence of the French element in Canada. I have chosen to speak about it for two reasons. The first one is that we Canadians of French language and descent do not wish to be considered as second-rate citizens by anyone or any country. We are Canadians deeply attached to the whole of our Canadian motherland. Because of their past and present endeavours we have a never-failing admiration and affection for our countrymen of English language and culture. We do not, however, intend to renounce our treasure of tradition, customs, culture and language, nor our slight oddities we know so well, for we are ready to accept all this from the other Canadians with whom we are in every way on equal standing.
The second reason is that I have been humiliated to see a United States congressman so ill-informed on Canadians of French descent. I told myself that it was up to the government of the province of Quebec to set the facts right and see that this beautiful

section of Canada is shown in a different light. It is the task of the federal government to give Canada a policy and economy which will give this country a standing in the world, whereas the provincial legislature must provide a policy which will give the province a standing in its immediate surroundings, Canadian and American.
The province of Quebec is the keeper of French culture. It behooves it to present it in its true light in Canada and the United States. The real flag of Quebec is its language, its well-spoken language; its French culture, a real culture coming from the best and purest sources; and its traditions of nobleness, affability and generosity. The French achievement in Canada is a fact. It is up to the government of Quebec to stress it within the Canadian confederation. I would suggest to this government that it could forget somewhat industrial development and turn its attention to cultural progress, which comprises both language and knowledge. It has been said, and I quote:
Production, after all, is not the goal of life. Production is only a means. God has not created man for the purpose of industrial production. Man has been created so that he should lead a healthy and comfortable life, and develop the faculties of his mind, in order to render the world more beautiful by the fact that it is lived in by man. We must bring production back to its proper value, when we consider the sense of life.
The Canadian of French origin must not only keep his language, culture and faith, but embellish and improve these three attributes of French individuality.
The part of Quebec in confederation will depend in far larger measure upon the perfection of its language, the clarity of its culture, the serenity and straightforwardness of its faith than upon industrial productivity. I am not opposed to industrial progress. It is necessary, and I make no difficulty about favouring it as long as this does not entail sacrificing upon the altar of the golden calf the admirable traditions left us by our fathers.
I know too that the legislature might have to defend and protect the rights and duties born of those traditions and provided for in the constitution. If ever the autonomy of a province is threatened I feel sure this house will rise in a body to demand that the constitution be respected, whichever province might be involved. The British House of Commons has ever jealously guarded those liberties issuing from the Magna Carta. The Canadian Commons will no less jealously defend the constitution.
There is a danger of essential truths being forgotten if we keep up this politicking
The Address-Mr. Boisvert founded on half truths. What we must seek first of all is to form true Canadians, proud of the part they are called upon to play in confederation-confederation having been agreed upon for this very reason- which consists in building up a fine and noble nation, joining two languages, two cultures which will ensure Canada's greatness and its influence throughout the whole world.
One word now about the United Nations. From my experience at the eighth session of the world assembly I have formed impressions, opinions and observations which will be of undoubted value to me. I have tried to get the greatest amount of benefit from my experience there as a political observer. This title is as yet very ill-defined, to such an extent that the best course to follow would seem to keep watch upon ourselves, first and foremost, and to remain everywhere and on all occasions perfectly reserved.
The United Nations is a human institution whose business it is not to frame laws but to promote peace and understanding in the world. The charter which is the basis for this peculiar organization is in the nature of a treaty. Sixty countries have signed and ratified the charter, thus binding themselves by its terms. Twenty other nations, so far, have asked to be admitted to the United Nations. There are thirteen trusteeship territories whose administration is the responsibility of the trusteeship council of the United Nations. We must add to this sixty other territories dependent upon other nations which, according to the charter, must provide information on the political, economic and social evolution of these territories. By its very nature the charter is destined to be universally applied.
Its possibilities are therefore infinite, on condition that world opinion ascribe to it a supranational usefulness in order that its decisions, accepted and admitted by the member nations, shall eventually become accepted as the basis for a new international law no longer used to frame treaties to end wars, but rather to prevent wars altogether and to bring about a fair and enduring peace.
The United Nations are struggling with three currents which undermine them. The first is unconcern. A good many people, here and there in the world, because they are not cognizant of the goals and aims of the organization, firmly believe that the United Nations are doing nothing. The second is indifference. This feeling is evident in the United States. The American masses take no interest in the organization. It is quite true that the United
436	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Boisvert Nations have neither baseball, hockey nor football teams. That indifference is distressing, for these people- have not yet realized the importance of that world stage and they do not understand that in order to be effective it must have the backing of public opinion. The third is contempt. Important people in the realm of politics, trade or industry state, "The United Nations is a worthless thing. We give away millions upon millions with no other result than being laughed at by the Russians and setting up small nations which will ultimately bleed us white without being at all thankful to us."
Lord Beaverbrook said on October 19:
Tile foreign secretaries of the great nations cannot keep still. They travel. The moral is: keep them at home and send our trade ministers abroad. Evacuate the United Nations and don't meddle any more in the domestic affairs of foreigners.
The noble lord was just reflecting the state of mind of too many people. I am glad the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) expressed in this house on the 20th a viewpoint totally different from the above.
These currents are dangerous, and they are a threat to the very existence of this world organization. The latter is not known well enough. Only if universal public opinion breathes life into it will it be able to survive. Nothing survives, nothing can survive, without the support of public opinion. The United Nations has been established for the promotion of peace, not for the preparation for war.
One finds in chapter I, article 1 of the charter the goals and the underlying principles of the organization. The purposes of the United Nations are: 1, to maintain international peace and security, etc.; 2, to develop friendly relations among nations, etc.; 3, to achieve international co-operation in solving international problems of an economic, social, cultural or humanitarian character, etc. Those principles follow from the preamble of the charter of the United Nations, agreed upon in San Francisco in 1945 and already, as I have pointed out, ratified by 60 nations. Here is the wording of this preamble:
1.	To maintain international peace and security, and to that end: to take effective collective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace, and for the suppression of acts of aggression or other breaches of the peace, and to bring about by peaceful means, and in conformity with the principles of justice and international law, adjustment or settlement of international disputes or situations which might lead to a breach of the peace;
2.	To develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples, and to take other appropriate measures to strengthen universal peace;


3.	To achieve international co-operation in solving international problems of an economic, social, cultural, or humanitarian character, and in promoting and encouraging respect for human rights and for fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language, or religion; and
4.	To be a centre for harmonizing the actions of nations in the attainment of these common ends.
The wording of the preamble may be romantic, but it is most inspiring and should be learned by heart by all the children of the world for, once grown up, those children who have known nothing of the horrors of war forget that their parents or their grandparents were victims of the violence of armed men.
Since the first session, thanks to the United Nations, peaceful solutions have been found in the dispute between India and Pakistan, who were at war for the possession of Kashmir. Other peaceful solutions have been found for the state of Israel and the neighbouring Arab countries, who have agreed to an armistice. Eritrea and Ethiopia have agreed to unite under the same government; and for the first time in history oppression has been repelled, in Korea, by the united armies of 16 nations who had signed the charter. Many other problems have been dealt with, not without enormous difficulty, and a ground of settlement was found which will be an asset for the world.
The United Nations may never take any speedy action, for it is not endowed with the sovereignty which is the prerogative of the member nations. These states must, in regard to questions of interest to them, take into account the public opinion prevailing among the people they govern. Such, for example, is the case of Trieste, of Tunisia and of Morocco. Many of these questions are deeply rooted in history, from which it would be difficult to cut them off violently. Diplomacy, which is the most refined and polished form of human relations, must be convincing in order to maintain links, or reestablish them when they are broken, between nations who are on the verge of cutting each other's throats for motives which very often are based on sentiment rather than on reason. The essential function of the United Nations is not to do away with diplomacy altogether but, on the contrary, to guide it, direct it, and emphasize its action with a view to peaceful solutions.

Thank you very much. Speaking before the United Nations, on September 23, 1953, our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) stated:
I know that without the active participation of world agencies of communication and information, this experiment in world organization could not succeed, because it would not be able to secure popular support. But the United Nations has, or should have, a private as well as a public face. There should be opportunities here for other than public appearances. A television panel discussion can be instructive and entertaining, but it is no substitute for direct consultation or for that old-fashioned diplomacy which is becoming more respectable by comparison with some of the gaudier, but not always more responsible or restrained successors.
To these appropriate words, I should like to add those of the new secretary, Mr. Hammarskjold, published in the annual report of the United Nations:
The work of the United Nations should always be viewed as a continuing process over a long period of time in which there is constant change and development. It is difficult to measure the significance of results in the perspective of any single year. Often the unspectacular or the unnoticed may prove to be a significant forward step on the long road toward peace in a world of organized co-operation and of more special partnership among nations.
The notion of speed in the Americans is such that they misunderstand the interplay of diplomacy and slow action exerted by the United Nations. Consequently it sometimes happens that they take a stand on most important questions which even their own friends can hardly understand. They will have to show a greater discretion, a better sense of diplomacy, a greater respect for the opinions of other nations. They will also have to learn how to better protect official secrets from the press which might be too eager for news, true or false, as well as from politicians who think that even friends should always be at daggers drawn.
I believe Russia wants to stay within the United Nations, as I believe that, should there be another war, Russia would spare Europe- I imagine that is part of her military strategy -in order to bring it to communism, but would pounce upon America with her atomic weapons and try, through a punitive action which would be truly hellish, to bring despair to the soul of America. If the European nations do not attack, Russia will not move against them.
We must be ready for such an alternative and prepare our defence accordingly. The north does not frighten the Russian armies. We may see the day-and would to heaven that men could find the spiritual strength to make
The Address-Mr. Blackmore peace-when European armies will be called upon to come to the help of our continent. Then we should, in Asia, conclude strong alliances so that, should Russia attack, we could take a short-cut, the shortest possible, to invade Russia on her south flank.
Oh, I suppose I am talking about matters which should not be talked about, but it is my humble opinion that we should be ready at all times to face any situation similar to the ones I have just mentioned.
I want to conclude on a more pleasant note. I was deeply moved by the election of Madame Pandit to the high position of president of the United Nations. When I met her I was struck with her pleasant features, her beautiful eyes expressive of all the poetry and spirituality of India; and when I saw her discharging her duties I marvelled at the natural authority emanating from her person. I then remembered that in the United Kingdom last June a young woman had been crowned queen of an empire and at the same time queen of our country. This half century will be marked by the promotion of women not only in national but in international affairs. Such a trend is apt to give us confidence in a humanity which is said to have become more and more barbarous.
The new role given to women may very well mark the end of wars, because this promotion which has been accepted by men will take on more and more importance. Women directing their natural heroism toward the promotion of peace may well succeed where men have failed. I pay tribute to our Queen and to Madame Pandit, and also to the United Nations for the work they are doing in order to further a fair, honourable and permanent peace. We can help and we will help if we apply to ourselves first and if we ask the other nations in the United Nations to remember always what Richelieu said about treaties:
Kings must be very careful about the treaties they sign but once they are concluded they must be religiously respected.

I desire to defend Senator McCarthy against the attack which the hon. member for Spadina made against him on November 23. I think probably I would be completely justified in doing this if there were no other ground than that the attack was made against

The Address-Mr. Blackmore a man who has no chance whatsoever to appear in this chamber to defend himself against it.
I was very desirous of having the hon. member for Spadina here and in order to ensure that he might be here, not knowing that of necessity he would be in Toronto, I wrote him the following letter which I think it advisable to put on the record. It is dated November 26, 1953, and reads as follows:
Mr. D. A. Croll, M.P.
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Croll:
On November 23rd you gave a speech in the House of Commons dealing with so-called McCarthy-ism. You took a strong position against United States Senator Joseph McCarthy, which I feel was your right and privilege as a responsible member of parliament.
In certain press interviews which I gave as a result of the question of the use of my frank by my secretary, Miss Moore, in sending to the Calgary Herald, together with two other documents, a copy of the magazine American Mercury, September 1953 issue, containing an article entitled: "The truth about Joe McCarthy"-in certain of such press interviews I used concerning Senator McCarthy words which are reported in the following quotation from the Toronto Globe and Mail, Friday, November 20, 1953, page 2:
"Mr. Blackmore described Senator McCarthy as 'the greatest fighter, the most militant and the most effective, against communism that we have in America today.'
The books advertised in the franked letter were While You Slept by John T. Flynn and The Iron Curtain Over America by John Beaty. Mr. Black-more praised them as exposures of communism in high places.
'If there is one thing that needs to be known today' he said, 'it is who is at the bottom of this communism in America, who is supplying the money? If true conditions in the United States, and they are probably the same in Canada, were known, certainly no one here would vote to support them.'
It was an outrage, Mr. Blackmore said, that University of Toronto students should have burned Senator McCarthy in effigy.
'Why did those boys and girls do that?' he asked. 'It was because they are so horribly deceived.' "

I am writing this letter to give you an opportunity to be in the house while I speak against the position which you took on November 23rd.
With admiration for you personally, and with warm regards,
Sincerely yours,

In beginning to discuss this matter I desire to make it clear, Mr. Speaker, that I do not propose to defend McCarthyism. I do not know whether there is such a thing as McCarthyism except in the hectic imagination of certain hysterical people and the newspapers of our time. I have some evidence as to what and who Senator Joseph McCarthy is, what his aims and achievements are and what his methods are. I have been unable to find any reliable evidence as to what McCarthyism is, and I invite all hon. members who think they have been so able to bring forth their evidence. They will have plenty of opportunity to talk after I sit down, and they d'o not need to sneer until they get the facts. What I have in mind is the meaning and definition associated with the word by former President Truman in the passage quoted from the Globe and Mail of November 17, 1953, as recorded at page 237 of Hansard for November 23, in the remarks of the hon. member for Spadina. The hon. member for Spadina quoted Truman as follows:
It is the corruption of truth, the abandonment of our historical devotion to fair play.
It is the abandonment of the due process of law.
It is the use of the big lie and the unfounded accusation against any citizen in the name of Americanism or security.
It is the rise to power of the demagogue who lives on untruth.
It is the spread of fear and the destruction of faith in every level of our society.

I am very much interested to see the reaction in the house. Now let us go on. I do not hesitate, Mr. Speaker, to defy any member in the house to establish the truthfulness of any remark former President Truman made concerning Senator McCarthy. If anyone can, he is welcome to do so and he has the whole of this session ahead of him to do so. Take the facts concerning Senator McCarthy as they are and as they can be discovered in great abundance, and I will defy any man to prove one single sentence in that statement to be true. I defy him to give evidence that will satisfy anyone who is not blinded by prejudice that there is truth in any of Truman's remarks thus quoted, if applied to Senator McCarthy.
Now, that is clear enough. Anyone who thinks he can rise to the occasion is invited to do so.
Neither do I propose to defend McCarthy-ites. I know of no McCarthyite, either in the United States or Canada. If there is anyone who can point to a McCarthyite and establish the case, I will be listening to him. We have

the word loosely used by people who do not know anything about the matter, except what they have gathered in a prejudiced way from reading some report. I repeat that I have some evidence relative to Senator Joseph McCarthy. I stand ready to defend Senator McCarthy on the basis of what I have been able thus far to read about him and learn about him. The terms "McCarthyism" and "McCarthyite" I leave to the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). Those two terms and the concepts of "McCarthyism" and "McCarthyite", as he has used them, have nothing whatever to do with Senator McCarthy.
Senator Joseph McCarthy, as I have discovered him, is a gentlemanly, patient, patriotic young fellow, a distinguished veteran of world war II. You did not hear that before? It is time you did. He is a distinguished veteran of world war II who faithfully offered his life in battle for the United States against fascism and nazism. He is a responsible Republican senator from the sovereign state of Wisconsin, and is now devotedly offering his life once more, this time in a fight for the United States against communism abroad, and particularly at home.
In support of my position I produce two witnesses today. The first is Igor Gouzenko. In the Toronto Telegram of November 21, 1953 there is an article on page 18 by Eugene Griffin. I may say that Eugene Griffin is a reporter for the Chicago Tribune press service, and I think a responsible man. From that article I quote these words of Gouzenko:
"Senator McCarthy is doing important patriotic work," Gouzenko said. "If he or Senator Jenner (R. Ind.) or their committees feel that I might be of assistance in their anti-communist investigations, I would be glad to help. I think a talk with them would be worth while."
Farther down in the article I find this:
Before he came to Canada, Gouzenko was a Russian army officer with training in espionage work as a specialist in codes, a role that made him cognizant of some of Moscow's deepest international intrigues. He worked one year in the Red army's main intelligence office, where he handled spy reports from communist agents in many countries.
This is a man whose opinion is not to be laughed off lightly. The article goes on, and I quote from Gouzenko:
"I saw a tremendous number of secret reports from the United States-tremendous," he said today. "They included all kinds of material, military information, plans, texts of secret American documents, and so on."
The question, Mr. Speaker, that the members of this house have got to ask themselves is, how, and from what agencies in the United States did Russia obtain these secrets?
The Address-Mr. Blackmore Until we can state that, and prove it, we had better be rather humble. I presume that man knows what he is talking about more than any member in this house can expect to know in regard to this matter.
In support of my position, as I said, I produce the witness Igor Gouzenko. As the second witness I produce a Catholic priest in an article entitled "Senator Joseph McCarthy", in which article he quotes an article by an eminent United States Catholic journalist, the Reverend Father James M. Gillis, C.S.P. I believe this is another man we had better not try to laugh off. The priest's article appears in No. 29 of the highly respected periodical Fiat. I am sorry to impose on the house a lengthy quotation, but there are going to be hundreds of thousands of people in this country who will not have an opportunity of reading this article. I am going to put it on the record so people who desire to get the facts may read it.
